questions.question: How do browser cookies work?
questions.title: How browser cookies work
questions.direct_answer: A cookie is a small name-value record stored by the browser for a site. A server usually creates it with Set-Cookie, and the browser later sends matching cookies in the Cookie request header according to scope, expiry, security attributes, and privacy rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the HTTP cookie request-response lifecycle.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing cookies as server storage or assuming every cookie is sent to every request.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Cookie values are controlled by the client and have tight size limits; sensitive application data should remain on the server.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A response can create a cookie with the Set-Cookie header.
The browser stores it and sends matching cookies in later Cookie headers.
Domain, Path, SameSite, Secure, and expiry rules limit when it is sent.
Cookies are client-held data, so the server must not blindly trust their values.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- A cookie is a small name-value record that a browser stores for a website. The common lifecycle begins when a server returns a `Set-Cookie` response header, after which the browser may attach that cookie to later requests in the `Cookie` header.

- Attachment is automatic only when the request matches the cookie's rules. The browser checks its host or Domain, Path, expiry, Secure flag, SameSite setting, and the user's privacy policy before sending it.

- For example, a server can set an opaque session ID after login. On the next matching HTTPS request, the browser sends that ID, and the server uses it to find session data held on the server.

- Cookies add bytes to matching HTTP requests, have small implementation limits, and can be changed or deleted by a user. They are suitable for identifiers and small preferences, not large records or trusted authorization facts.

- A cookie is therefore a browser-managed transport mechanism; its safety depends on narrow scope, secure attributes, expiry, and server-side validation.

sections.title: A cookie crosses the HTTP boundary
sections.content: The server cannot place data directly into browser memory. It sends instructions in `Set-Cookie`, the user agent decides whether to accept them, and later requests carry eligible values in `Cookie`. This round trip is what lets stateless HTTP requests participate in a stateful login or remember a small preference.

sections.title: Scope and lifetime decide eligibility
sections.content: Omitting Domain creates a host-only cookie; adding Domain can make it available to matching subdomains. Path limits which request paths receive it but is not a security boundary against reading. A cookie without Max-Age or Expires is a session cookie, while an explicit lifetime allows persistence. Browser privacy settings, storage clearing, and cookie policies can still shorten or block that lifetime.

sections.title: Cookie request cycle
sections.content:
Browser → Server: POST /login
Server → Browser: Set-Cookie: session=abc; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Browser: store cookie after policy checks
Browser → Server: GET /account + Cookie: session=abc
Server: look up session abc and authorize the request

sections.title: Set a narrow session cookie on the server
sections.content:
```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=1800
```
The `__Host-` prefix requires HTTPS, `Path=/`, and no Domain attribute in supporting browsers.

questions.question: What do Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite do on a cookie?
questions.title: Cookie security attributes
questions.direct_answer: Secure limits a cookie to HTTPS requests, HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading it through document.cookie, and SameSite controls when it is sent with cross-site requests. These protections complement each other but do not replace XSS and CSRF defenses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the separate threat addressed by each cookie attribute.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling Secure encryption, treating HttpOnly as complete XSS protection, or treating SameSite as a complete CSRF solution.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: SameSite=None requires Secure; legitimate cross-site flows may need None and additional CSRF protection.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Secure sends the cookie only over HTTPS requests.
HttpOnly hides the value from browser JavaScript APIs such as document.cookie.
SameSite limits inclusion on cross-site requests: Strict, Lax, or None.
SameSite=None must be paired with Secure, and no single flag solves every attack.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- The three attributes protect different parts of a cookie's journey. `Secure` restricts transmission to HTTPS, `HttpOnly` prevents page scripts from reading the value through `document.cookie`, and `SameSite` controls whether the browser includes it in cross-site requests.

- For example, a login session cookie commonly uses `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`. HTTPS protects it in transit, injected JavaScript cannot directly copy its value, and most cross-site background requests will not carry it.

- These controls are not interchangeable. Secure does not make the stored value encrypted, HttpOnly does not stop malicious script from sending authenticated same-site requests, and SameSite is only one layer of CSRF defense.

- `SameSite=Strict` is the narrowest but can interrupt links arriving from another site. `Lax` supports common top-level navigation, while `None` enables cross-site use and must also use Secure.

- A safe cookie chooses the narrowest practical scope and lifetime, then combines these attributes with output escaping, content security policy, CSRF defenses, and server-side session checks.

sections.title: Three controls, three boundaries
sections.content: Transport, script access, and request context are separate security questions. A cookie can travel only over HTTPS yet remain readable by JavaScript; it can be HttpOnly yet still ride on a cross-site request. Reading the attributes as independent gates prevents a false sense of safety.

sections.title: Why layered defenses still matter
sections.content: HttpOnly reduces session-token theft through XSS, but hostile code executing in the page can still act with the user's session. SameSite reduces many cross-site request paths, but applications with cross-site integrations may allow such traffic. Short expiry, session rotation, CSRF tokens or fetch-metadata checks, input handling, and a restrictive content security policy address parts that cookie flags do not cover.

sections.title: What each attribute controls
sections.content:
| Attribute | Controls | Does not guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Secure | HTTP versus HTTPS transport | Encryption at rest or XSS safety |
| HttpOnly | JavaScript access to the value | Blocking requests made by injected code |
| SameSite | Cross-site cookie inclusion | Complete CSRF protection |
| Max-Age / Expires | Lifetime | Immediate revocation on the server |

sections.title: A typical first-party session setting
sections.content:
```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=1800
```
A cross-site widget would need a different design and may require `SameSite=None; Secure`.
